newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Fresh clashes as Bangui awaits mediator.
newsitem.headline: Fresh clashes as Bangui awaits mediator.

text.p: Fresh clashes between African peacekeepers and disaffected soldiers shook parts of the Central African Republic capital Bangui on Monday as the city awaited the arrival of mediator Amadou Toumani Toure.

Witnesses reported a mini-exodus of several thousand residents fleeing their homes in the city for the security of the countryside, following clashes that began on Friday and have killed at least 30 people -- many of them civilians.
Peacekeepers deployed at key intersections with French troops, in the former French colony under a defence pact, deploying behind them, witnesses said.

French helicopters flew over the city and intermittent salvoes of mortar and heavy machine-gun fire could be heard from various districts. France said that its intervention was limited to supporting the peacekeepers.

"The French army is not intervening in the front line," its ambassador Jean-Marc Simon told French radio, adding that it was helping as needed. "There is of course no question of France dropping these friendly armies when they are in trouble."
Earlier, Mali's widely respected former military leader, Toumani Toure, who brokered a January peace deal, said he was returning to Bangui.

He expressed disappointment but said any solution to the clashes, which stem from political and ethnic rivalry between supporters and opponents of President Ange-Felix Patasse within the army, lay with Central African Republic citizens themselves.
"My role is to help the two parties, the different parties to agree," he told Radio France International in an interview. "The vital role will always come back to the nationals."

The Bangui peacekeeping force has been touted as a model for a solution in Brazzaville, capital of the neighbouring Congo Republic when similar political and ethnic clashes killed hundreds of people this month.
France intervened on Sunday to defend the African peacekeepers, who deployed in the city under the January pact to end a third army mutiny in under a year.
Around 70 people have been wounded in the fighting, including five French nationals who were hit on Saturday by two stray mortar bombs that fell on the French embassy compound.

The January 25 deal included a plan to reintegrate the mutineers into their units and then conduct general disarmament. Many mutineers had already rejoined their units but the process snagged this month on efforts to reintegrate members of the paramilitary gendarmerie.

Mutinies in April and May 1996 began as protests over pay but became a movement to topple Patasse, a northern civilian elected in 1993. The third mutiny began in November and degenerated into ethnic bloodshed.
Most of the mutineers are members of the Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba.
The French troops -- there are now 1,650 in the country -- restored order after the last mutiny and then handed over to the peacekeepers.
The 800-strong African force includes soldiers from Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo. A Senegalese soldier killed on Friday was among the first casualties of the flare-up.
